reading.title: Matching tools with their functions
reading.text: The trainee compares equipment rather than follows a recipe. A Champagne flute is tall and narrow; a beer mug has a mug shape. Collins glass is tall and straight-sided, whereas coupe glass has a shallow broad bowl. A snifter has a rounded bowl with a narrower opening. A cocktail shaker combines ingredients by shaking. A jigger measures quantities, a muddler presses ingredients, and a bar spoon stirs. A strainer separates solids, and ice tongs lift ice pieces. A bottle opener removes a closure, while a corkscrew specifically removes corks. A citrus press squeezes fruit; a zester removes thin outer-peel strips. The trainee checks the tool's purpose without assuming that its name fixes one serving size or that a glass identifies a beverage.

reading.title: Reading a staffing chart
reading.text: A fictional staffing chart identifies responsibilities. The bartender prepares and serves drinks, and the barback stocks and organizes the service area. Mixologist describes a specialist in mixed-drink development or preparation. A bouncer handles venue security; the title does not grant unlimited authority. The host welcomes guests. Cocktail waitress is a gendered term for a woman serving drinks; server is a neutral alternative. The manager coordinates operations. A sommelier specializes in wine selection and service. A DJ selects recorded music, while a promoter advertises or organizes events. Responsibilities vary by workplace, so the trainee reads the actual assignments. Clothing and a generic venue photograph cannot establish any of these roles. The lesson practices professional terminology without requiring attendance, consumption or participation in an event.
